segments: A solo technical founder who is three weekends into a homemade support chatbot that still has no logs, no cost tracking and no way to stop it saying something stupid
A two-person automation agency owner who has sold the same WhatsApp assistant to six clients and now maintains six separate codebases
A support/ops lead at a 30-person e-commerce company who personally answers the same forty emails every morning before she can start her real job
gaps: No customer names, quotes or case studies found - the copy can describe the product but cannot prove anyone uses it

business.what_it_does: A no-code platform for building custom AI agents (chatbots/assistants) powered by models like Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini — each agent bundles a model, a system prompt, a persona, a knowledge base, guardrails, and gets its own REST API endpoint, deployable via API, embeddable widget, or channels like Slack, WhatsApp, and Telegram.
business.category: AI agent platform / no-code AI chatbot & assistant builder
business.business_model: Subscription SaaS billed monthly, with each plan including a bundle of usage credits ("Payez uniquement ce que vous utilisez" — pay only for what you use); a free tier with starting credits, self-serve paid upgrades, and custom-priced Enterprise sold via sales contact.

voice.tone: Direct and benefit-first, sells on concrete numbers (credits, exécutions, latency, uptime) instead of adjectives; confident but plain — no hype words like 'revolutionary' or 'solution', just what it does and what it costs.
voice.rhythm: Short declarative sentences, often paired: a bold claim followed by a concrete, literal follow-up. Headlines are terse contrasts ('en quelques minutes, pas des semaines'). Clauses are frequently appended after an em dash rather than a comma.
voice.person: We/nous — the company speaks as the platform's builder ('nous gérons le routage...'), addresses the reader directly as 'vous'/'you', no individual name signs anything.

segments.name: A solo technical founder who is three weekends into a homemade support chatbot that still has no logs, no cost tracking and no way to stop it saying something stupid
segments.situation: He is the only engineer on a 4-person SaaS. A customer-facing assistant got promised on the roadmap call in January, so he wired the OpenAI SDK to a Postgres table, then added pgvector when the FAQ answers came back wrong, then added a retry loop when the provider 500'd during a demo. It half-works. What does not exist: per-request cost visibility (he found out the bill was $180 when Stripe emailed him), a way to see what users actually asked yesterday, any block on someone pasting 'ignore your previous instructions', and a session store that survives a redeploy. Every model announcement means another evening rewriting the client because the message format changed. He has a Notion page called 'agent infra TODO' with eleven items on it, and none of them are the product he is actually supposed to be building. His co-founder keeps asking why the chatbot is taking a month.
segments.job_to_be_done: Ship the assistant his roadmap promised and go back to building the actual product — without becoming the guy who maintains an in-house LLM platform for the next two years.
segments.trigger: A model deprecation email, a surprise provider bill, or a demo where the bot answered a prospect wrongly in front of the co-founder — whichever lands first in a given month.

pains.statement: He is maintaining a vector database he never wanted to run, purely so the bot can answer questions from a PDF.

provenance.quote: The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage.

pains.statement: Every provider swap means rewriting client code and juggling another SDK, so he is quietly locked into whichever model he integrated first.

provenance.source: orqagent.com homepage — Any LLM, One API
provenance.quote: Claude, GPT-4, Mistral, Llama, Gemini — switch models with a single field. No SDK juggling, no vendor lock-in.

pains.statement: The work he keeps doing is not the agent — it is routing, logs, billing and analytics around the agent, and none of it is differentiated.

provenance.quote: Apportez votre prompt — nous gérons le routage, les logs, la facturation et l'analytique.

pains.statement: He cannot answer 'what did this cost us last week and which model was it' without writing a reporting job first.
There is nothing between a hostile user and his system prompt; he knows it and has been putting off building it.
The 'few weeks' estimate he gave has already been wrong twice, and the credibility cost is worse than the engineering cost.

provenance.quote: Créez des agents IA en quelques minutes, pas des semaines

segments.name: A two-person automation agency owner who has sold the same WhatsApp assistant to six clients and now maintains six separate codebases
segments.situation: She runs a small francophone dev/automation shop. Clients are dentists, e-commerce shops, a driving school — each one wanted 'un chatbot qui répond aux clients'. She built the first in n8n plus a Python script, then copy-pasted it five times. Now client #3's Telegram bot is on an old prompt, client #5 wants their logo on the dashboard and she has been stalling because there is no dashboard, and every month she manually reconciles which client burned how many API tokens against what she invoiced them. Onboarding a new client is a four-day job that she can only charge two days for, so growth actively costs her margin. Her recurring revenue is real but her delivery does not scale, and the last two prospects asked questions about data handling she could not answer in writing.
segments.job_to_be_done: Turn a bespoke four-day build into a same-week deliverable she can resell under her own brand, so adding client seven does not add a maintenance burden she carries forever.
segments.trigger: A prospect asks for something she cannot deliver on the copy-paste stack — their own branding, a client login, a written answer on where the data lives — or a client churns because their bot silently broke and nobody noticed.

pains.statement: Six clients means six deployments to patch by hand; a prompt fix is a day of work instead of a field edit.
She cannot put her own brand in front of clients, so she is reselling someone else's tooling visibly, at agency prices.

provenance.quote: White-label the entire dashboard under your brand.

pains.statement: Per-client usage and cost are invisible until the provider bill arrives, so her margin on each retainer is a guess.
Clients want the bot where their customers already are — WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram — and each channel is a separate integration she has to build and babysit.

provenance.quote: Native integrations with the channels and tools your team already uses.

pains.statement: She has no written answer to 'is our client data used to train the model', which is now costing her deals with slightly larger prospects.

segments.name: A support/ops lead at a 30-person e-commerce company who personally answers the same forty emails every morning before she can start her real job
segments.situation: She is not a developer and has no engineering time allocated to her. The shared inbox gets 40–60 messages a day and roughly two-thirds are 'où est ma commande', 'quelle est votre politique de retour', 'ça existe en taille 42'. All the answers exist — in a returns policy PDF, a shipping FAQ and a spreadsheet nobody outside the team has read. Peak season doubles the volume and last November they paid for a temp who needed three weeks of training to be useful for six weeks of work. She has tried the canned-responses feature in the helpdesk; it saves keystrokes, not decisions. Someone showed her ChatGPT and she pasted a policy into it once, which worked beautifully and taught her nothing about how to make it happen 40 times a day without a person in the loop. Her genuine fear is not that it costs money — it is that an automated reply promises a refund the company does not offer and she finds out from a furious customer on Instagram.
segments.job_to_be_done: Get the repetitive two-thirds of the inbox handled accurately so the team can answer the hard third properly — and stop hiring seasonal temps to read the same FAQ out loud.
segments.trigger: Q4 volume planning, or a resignation on a two-person support team that makes the coming month obviously impossible.

pains.statement: The answers to most incoming questions already exist in documents; the cost is a human retyping them, not finding them.

provenance.quote: Upload PDFs, docs or plain text.

pains.statement: Any automation that replies without her seeing it first is unacceptable — one wrong refund promise costs more than the whole month of saved time.

provenance.quote: IMAP polling + SMTP replies, with a human approval queue.

pains.statement: She has no developer to assign this to and no budget line to hire one, so anything requiring 'just an API call' is dead on arrival.
Connecting anything to the live shared inbox terrifies her, because a bad setup could blast replies at every old thread in the archive.

provenance.quote: Messages older than 24 h are skipped — so connecting an inbox never replies to your whole archive.

pains.statement: Her mornings are gone before they start, and the strategic work she was actually hired for slides to evenings.

objections.objection: I'm a developer. This is a wrapper around an API call — I could build it myself in a weekend, and then I own it.
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and only by refusing to argue about the model call. The evidence says the weekend job is the call; the year-long job is everything around it — a dedicated REST endpoint with key auth per agent (E17), stateful sessions (E18), per-key usage caps and per-minute/per-day rate limits (E19, E47, E48), RAG over uploaded docs with no vector DB to run (E11), guardrails for PII/content/injection defined once and enforced every run (E13), P95 latency, per-model token usage, daily spend and guardrail trigger rates tracked with no extra config (E12), per-run USD cost and latency in the response body (E73, E74), run history with status filter (E21), eight channel integrations (E23), and serverless scaling with no infra (E22). Honest limit: nothing in the evidence quantifies the build-vs-buy gap in hours or money, so the copy has to enumerate rather than assert.

objections.objection: Your own pricing pages contradict each other. Pro is 10 agents / 20,000 executions on one page and unlimited agents on another; free is 100 executions on one page and 500 runs on a third. If I can't trust the pricing table, why would I trust the billing?
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence resolves this. The material genuinely carries three incompatible descriptions of the same $29 plan and two of the free plan, plus a credits-vs-executions dual currency that is never reconciled (a run consumes both, and it is never stated which one cuts you off first). This objection cannot be beaten with what we currently know — the copy must avoid stating specific plan limits at all, or the company must fix the tables before any email quotes a number beyond the $0 / $29 / $99 prices and the 1,500 signup credits.

objections.objection: Credits are an unpredictable second currency. I don't know what my month costs until it's over, and if I run out mid-month my production agent stops answering customers.
objections.answer: Only partly. In favour: every run returns an estimated USD cost to 6 decimals (E73), analytics show daily spend trends and token usage per model without config (E12), per-agent rate limits and per-key usage caps let you bound the blast radius (E19, E47, E48), BYOK means you can put the model spend on your own provider account instead (E4, E151), and the credit bundles are stated with a Sonnet-call equivalent (E131, E135, E140). Against, and it must be conceded rather than hidden: hitting the monthly run limit returns HTTP 429 QUOTA_EXCEEDED (E129) — the agent does stop — and no auto-top-up, overage rate or spend alert exists anywhere in the evidence.

objections.objection: Your retrieval is keyword scoring, not embeddings. On my documents that will miss the paraphrased question, which is the only kind of question real users ask.
objections.answer: Weakly answered, and only for a reader who will test rather than argue. The mechanism is stated plainly — ~500-token overlapping chunks, keyword scoring against the user message, top chunks injected into the system prompt (E56, E57, E58) — and it is inspectable rather than a black box: chunks_injected appears per run in analytics and in the API response (E61, E77), used_knowledge_base is returned per run (E76), and a database icon marks any Playground message that pulled context (E51). The free tier with 1,500 credits and no card lets them upload their own docs and find out in ten minutes (E25, E39, E120). Nothing in the evidence claims or measures retrieval quality, so the only honest move is to invite the test.

objections.objection: We can't route customer data through a vendor that isn't certified. SOC 2 'in progress' is not SOC 2.
objections.answer: Answerable for a startup buyer, not for a procurement-gated one. Available: encrypted in transit and at rest (E5), never used to train any model (E6), per-tenant isolation (E7), GDPR-ready with EU data residency (E8), API keys hashed at rest with JWT auth (E159), integration credentials AES-256-GCM encrypted and never returned to the browser (E89), key revocation, expiry and temporary disable (E63, E67, E68), PII masking guardrail (E13), RBAC and full audit logs (E14), and for Enterprise, dedicated infrastructure/VPC, custom LLM endpoints, SSO/SAML and an SLA (E35, E36, E34, E37, E147). What is missing is the certification itself — E159 concedes SOC 2 is only in progress. For a buyer whose security review requires the report, this stays blocking and no email fixes it.

objections.objection: I've never heard of you. No logos, no case studies, no funding, no track record — if you shut down in a year, my client's live chatbot dies with you and I'm the one who has to explain it.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. There is not a single customer name, testimonial, usage number, founding date, team page or funding fact in the entire material — the only social proof is the phrase 'Join developers building smarter products', which names nobody. The 99.9% uptime claim (E9) speaks to availability, not to company survival, and the SLA is Enterprise-only (E37, E147). The adjacent mitigations — BYOK so the model relationship stays yours (E4), and a portable pattern where each agent is just a REST endpoint you call (E17) — reduce the damage but do not answer the doubt. This is the single largest unaddressed risk for the agency segment and should be flagged upward as a missing-asset problem, not written around.

objections.objection: We already have something — a helpdesk with AI replies, or a ChatGPT Team subscription the team already uses. Ripping that out is not worth the disruption.
objections.answer: Barely answered by the evidence. The only real lever is that trying it costs nothing and displaces nothing: 1,500 credits, no card (E1, E25, E39), an agent configured in under two minutes (E24, E130), and it runs alongside what exists because it deploys into the channels already in use — Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram, Email Inbox, webhooks (E23) — rather than replacing the system of record. The differentiators a generic assistant lacks are a callable endpoint per agent (E17), enforced guardrails (E13), document-grounded answers with citations (E11, E59, E60) and per-run cost/latency analytics (E12, E73). There is no migration path, no importer, and no comparison anywhere in the material, so the honest ask is 'run one workflow beside it', never 'switch'.

objections.objection: If I let an AI answer customers unsupervised it will eventually promise something we don't offer, and that costs me more than the time it saves.
objections.answer: This one is well answered — it is arguably the strongest thing in the evidence. Auto-reply is off by default, so drafts land in an approval queue with status pending_approval for review, edit, then Send or Ignore (E102, E111); reply_requires_approval defaults to ON to keep a human in the loop (E112); guardrails block injection attempts, violence/self-harm content and profanity above a threshold (E85, E86, E87), return HTTP 400 and log blocked_by_guardrail so block rates are visible (E88, E79); automated senders like no-reply and mailer-daemon are skipped (E104); messages over 24 hours old are skipped so connecting an inbox never replies to the archive (E105); each message is processed exactly once, idempotent on Message-ID (E106); answers can be constrained to uploaded documents and cite them (E11, E59); Constraints and response-format/JSON-schema fields hard-bound what it may say (E45, E46); and every run is inspectable with full history and status filtering (E21).

objections.objection: This is sold as no-code but the documentation is curl commands, API keys, JSON schemas and IMAP ports. It's clearly built for developers, and I don't have one.
objections.answer: Answerable, but only by leading with the console path and never showing a code block to this reader. Evidence: it is described as a no-code platform where you write a system prompt, pick a model and configure guardrails and tools entirely from the console in under two minutes (E24, E130); persona is set with plain fields — role, tone, language, constraints, welcome message (E44); a chat widget is one snippet for any site (E156); the Email Inbox is configured per agent in its own tab with no environment variables required (E98); Telegram is a pasted BotFather token with the webhook registered automatically (E91), Slack and Notion and Google Docs are OAuth installs (E90, E94, E95), and channel callbacks are wired up by the dashboard so no URLs are pasted by hand (E96); the Playground is a chat window for iterating before going live (E50, E51). The docs' centre of gravity remains the REST API, and no non-technical walkthrough exists in the material.

objections.objection: White-labelling is on your feature list, but can I actually hand a client a dashboard with my name on it — my domain, my login, their data separated from my other clients?
objections.answer: Half answered. Confirmed: the entire dashboard can be white-labelled under your brand (E15), collaborators can be invited with role-based permissions and full audit logs (E14), tenants are separated by design (E7), and Pro includes white-label plus Teams & RBAC at $29 (E30, E31). Not answered anywhere in the evidence: a custom domain, client-facing sub-accounts, per-client billing separation, or reselling terms. Stripe Billing appears only as an integration in the list (E23) with no detail. An agency asking the precise version of this question will not find the answer in the material.

objections.objection: Unlimited agents for $29 is too cheap to be real. Where is the catch, and what happens on the invoice at month three?
objections.answer: The catch is real, nameable, and better said out loud: the plan price buys a credit bundle, not unlimited usage. Pro is $29/month with 30,000 credits, stated as roughly 1,100 Sonnet calls (E30, E123, E135); the agent count is what is unlimited, not the runs (E31, E124). Free is 1,500 credits, about 55 Sonnet calls (E131). Playground testing burns the same quota as production (E54), and channel messages are real billed runs too (E97, E78). Naming this before the reader finds it converts the objection into a trust signal; hiding it makes the first invoice a churn event.

objections.objection: I'm mid-quarter with a shipping deadline. Even if this is better, evaluating it is a week I don't have.
objections.answer: Answered by shrinking the ask rather than arguing urgency: signup is free with no card (E1, E39), sign-up to first API call is documented as under five minutes and agent creation as under two (E24, E130), the Playground tests the exact live configuration — same model, prompt and knowledge base — before any code is written (E50), and the endpoint is a single POST from any language with no SDK to install (E17). The realistic first step is one agent over one document, not a migration.
